1:
Ellicott begins with the grammar. The verb is I saw, not I looked, and the tense of the participle is perfect: John did not watch a door swing open, he saw that a door already stood open. Robertson confirms the reading from the participle itself, and adds that it is the same verb used of the door of opportunity set before Philadelphia and the door of the heart on which Christ knocks — here, he says, the door of revelation. Robertson also insists that the opening phrase marks a change in the panorama rather than in the chronology, so that what follows need not come after the seven letters in time. Wesley builds a whole structural principle on the same words: throughout this book and joins the parts of the prophecy while after these things divides them, and John writes down one part after another as he sees and hears it.

Wesley notices that the openings widen as the book proceeds — a door here, the temple of God in heaven later, and at last heaven itself — each granting a new and more extended prospect. Ellicott sets the scene against its predecessors: in Ezekiel, and at the baptism, the heavens divide, whereas here a door simply stands open, and it stands open still, so that all who have faith may enter. Victorinus, writing earliest of these, reads the open door as the announcement of the new covenant: it was previously closed to men and was fully laid open when Christ ascended with His body to the Father. He then turns the trumpet voice into an argument. Because it is the same voice John had already heard, the one who now speaks is the one who spoke in the prophets, which condemns those who say that one spoke in the prophets and another in the Gospel. Henry draws a discipline from the same door rather than a doctrine: whatever is transacted on earth is first settled in heaven, we can know of it only what God is pleased to discover, and we must not intrude into the secret of His presence but wait until we are called up to it. Those who improve the discoveries already given, he adds, are thereby prepared for more.

On the mode of the vision the voices divide. Gill says plainly that the looking was done with the eyes of the mind and not of the body, which is why the prophets are called seers and their prophecies visions; he leaves the interval since the first vision undetermined, perhaps only a few minutes. Henry agrees that bodily actions and sensations were for a time suspended, the body being a veil and a clog to the mind in its dealings with God. Barnes canvasses the options at length — that the scenes passed before the mind with nothing visible, that they were so presented that John could copy them, or that they were the author's imagination, which he reports as the view chiefly held by German writers — and concludes that no representation to the bodily eye need be supposed, though the symbols were real as a delineation of coming events, for otherwise the visions are as worthless as dreams. He is willing to allow that John may have understood no more of them than his readers, his office being an accurate transcript, as a man may copy the devices of heraldry or the cuneiform of Persepolis without knowing their meaning. Against all of them Clarke states flatly that this was a visible aperture in the sky over John's head.
2:
Robertson notes that John had already come to be in the Spirit at the start of the book, so the phrase here is not a fresh entrance but a result: at once he found himself in the Spirit. Gill takes it the other way, supposing he had been for some little time out of his ecstasy and now returned to it, and he records that the Arabic version reads instead that he went in the Spirit — that is, in obedience to the voice that called him up. Wesley says only that it was in a higher degree than before, and Ellicott, comparing Paul caught up to the third heaven, describes mind and soul absorbed in the vision. Barnes is careful about what is not claimed: John does not say he was caught up into heaven, and was doubtless still on Patmos.

The throne, both Ellicott and Robertson insist, was not seen being set; when John saw, it was already in place, the first thing in heaven. Barnes takes the words in heaven as decisive against those who made the scene the temple at Jerusalem, since no temple imagery appears anywhere in it; Isaiah had his vision in the holy place and Ezekiel his by the Chebar, but John looks directly into heaven. That the occupant of the throne is never named strikes several of them as deliberate. Barnes finds it remarkable that no description is given from which a picture or an image could be formed, and reads this as a guard against idolatry; Ellicott wonders whether it is a touch of the Jewish reluctance to name God, or whether the standing phrase He that sat on the throne is kept before us through the whole book to remind us that the world’s drama moves under the eyes of the ruling One; Robertson likewise calls the participle a substitute for the divine name on the Hebrew pattern, and warns that all of this is glorious imagery and not actual objects in heaven, since God is spirit. Clarke says simply that the description aims at the surrounding glory rather than at the person of the King. Wesley alone turns the throne into a programme for reading the book: it is the centre from which everything in the visible world goes forth and to which it returns, and where commentators divide into the theological and the historical, the right way is to join both.

What colour the jasper was they cannot settle. Barnes leaves it undesignated but infers red, since red was the colour worn by princes, so that the enthroned One appeared as a prince in scarlet robes. Wesley makes it transparent and glittering white with an intermixture of colours, a symbol of purity. Gill reports it as variously coloured, the most valued sort green spotted with red or purple, and cites the Aramaic renderings of the breastplate stone which name it for the panther because of its spots. Ellicott concedes that the best authorities call jasper a dark opaque green, then argues that such a stone would combine badly with the red sardius and the green bow, and appeals to the later description of a jasper clear as crystal for a brighter stone whose brightness and flame signify holiness and righteousness. Robertson cuts across all of it: the word covers stones of quite different colours, some even take it for the diamond, and it is certainly not the cheap modern stone of that name. On the bow they agree. Barnes reads it as the emblem of peace after storm and of the covenant set in the cloud, abiding calmly above the lightnings; Ellicott has it encircling the throne completely, mercy encompassing judgment; Robertson, a complete circle; Wesley, green for favour to the good, and its breadth fixing the distance of those who stood about the throne.
4:
Barnes objects to the English word seats: the Greek is the same word used of the great throne itself, and since these figures wear crowns of gold the translation ought to have kept the royal sense. Ellicott makes the same complaint and guesses at its motive — perhaps the translators wished to reserve the word for Him who sat in the midst — but points out that the same persons are afterwards called kings and priests. Robertson adds that the manuscripts divide over the case of the nouns here, some reading a nominative and others an accusative that requires the verb I saw to be supplied from the opening verse.

Why twenty-four is the question that occupies them all. Gill sees the seats arranged in a semicircle answering to the bow, and describes the seating of a Jewish court, where the prince sat highest with the father of the court at his right hand and a sage at his left while the rest curved before them; but he concedes that the numbers do not agree, the greater council having seventy-one and the lesser twenty-three. Clarke offers that lesser council of twenty-three as one possibility and the twenty-four courses of priests appointed by David as another, takes the white raiment for priestly garments and the crowns as an emblem of dignity, and quotes a rabbinic passage in which a soul before birth is carried into paradise and shown the righteous crowned. Ellicott gathers the proposals — the twelve tribes doubled, so that Jew and Gentile are joined; two sets of twelve for the two Testaments; the twelve patriarchs with the twelve apostles — and argues that these are all the same thought in different dress, namely the complete Church of God in both Testaments, the spiritual successors of those priestly courses. Robertson canvasses the same suggestions and declines them: we do not really know why the number was chosen, and he is willing to add the possibility of an angelic rank about which nothing is known. He also observes that John elsewhere uses a different word for the kingly diadem, though he doubts the old distinction between diadem and victor’s wreath was still firmly kept.

On what the elders are, most of the voices converge. Barnes lays out his conclusion in numbered steps: they are of a kingly order, they are emblematic rather than a literal count of the heavenly host, they are of our race and not angels, they are the redeemed who say that they were purchased by blood out of every kindred and tongue, and therefore they represent the whole Church of every land and age in its triumph, crowned and harping. Ellicott notes what is easy to miss, that in the corresponding vision of Ezekiel no human beings appear at all, so that their presence here is itself significant: these are the friends of Christ, admitted to know what their Lord does. Wesley calls them the most holy of all the former ages, representing the whole body of the saints, seated in general but falling down when they worship, their white robes and gold crowns proving that they have already finished their course. He then presses a point none of the others raise: they are never called souls, from which he judges it probable that they already possessed glorified bodies.
5:
Ellicott catches a change of tense that the English hides: the lightnings and thunderings and voices do not merely proceed, they proceed continually. He then heads off a common reading. Some take them for signals of judgments about to fall; it is better, he argues, to take them as the standing tokens of a power that can show itself in judgment, which is what the clouds and lightnings at Sinai were, and what the psalm means by saying that righteousness and judgment are the habitation of His throne. Robertson agrees on the force of the tense, calling it a vivid present, and notes that the same three nouns recur later in the book though not always in the same order; the thunderstorm, he observes, is a familiar emblem of divine power in Hebrew poetry. Barnes reaches for Sinai as well, where there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud, and reinforces it with Milton’s chariot of Paternal Deity flashing thick flames. He suspects that voices standing next to thunders may simply name the rolling, re-echoing sound of the thunder itself. Wesley divides the three by the senses they assault — the lightnings reach the sight, the voices the hearing, the thunderings make the whole body tremble — and then reverses the expected effect: weak men account it terrible, but to the inhabitants of heaven it is a source of joy mixed with reverence, and to the saints on earth it conveys light and protection, however it may strike their enemies.

Over the seven lamps the agreement breaks. Robertson insists on the word: these are not the lampstands of the first chapter nor a household lamp fed with oil, but torches, and they blaze perpetually before the throne. He identifies them, as the verse itself does, with the seven Spirits of God. Barnes takes the same identification and works out what it might signify: that the Spirit’s operations are all of the nature of light, dissipating darkness and quickening what they touch; and that the placing of these steady flames in the very midst of the thunder and lightning pictures the Spirit shining calmly through every storm on earth, every convulsion of empire and every commotion raised in the soul by the thunders of the law. Ellicott, pressing the emblem of fire, denies that it need be fire of judgment only, since the baptism of the Spirit is a baptism of fire that purges and consumes evil; and he offers a suggestion the others do not make, that the torches recall the lamp of fire that passed between the divided pieces in the covenant with Abraham. If that is right, he says, three covenant tokens stand together in this one scene: the bow of Noah, the flaming torches of Abraham, and the thunderings of Sinai. Clarke breaks with all of them and reads the seven lamps of fire as seven angels, the attendants and ministers of the supreme King.
6:
Robertson begins with the adjective: the sea is glassy, which describes an appearance and not a material, and the crystal it resembles is clear rock-crystal rather than anything semi-opaque. He recalls that the elders on Sinai saw under God’s feet a paved work of sapphire, and suggests the likeness of sky to sea lies behind the image. Barnes works from the same physical sense — a pellucid expanse stretched out like an ocean — and thinks it is the pavement on which the throne stood; it may signify the vastness of God’s empire, or the placid calm of His administration, though he warns against pressing such details too far for symbolic meaning. Gill is the most combative. He rules out heaven itself, the souls of the blessed, the angelic host and the first Jerusalem converts, on the ground that the victors are later said to stand upon this sea; he reports the reading that takes it for the world, since waters in this book mean peoples, glass their frailty and crystal the openness of all things to God’s eye; and he rejects it, because the world is never likened to a still sea but to a troubled one whose waters cast up mire and dirt. Ellicott builds on exactly that contrast: the harlot sits on many waters which are peoples and multitudes and nations, the fickle and stormy sea of world opinion, whereas this sea is never in storm but only interfused with flame, and stands for the counsels of God, often fathomless but never obscure. Its position, he adds, answers to that of the molten sea before Solomon’s temple. Wesley alone identifies it: since the Spirit is figured under emblems of both fire and water, the seven torches and this sea may equally mean the seven Spirits of God, and so may the river of water of life that flows out of the throne later in the book.

Where the living creatures stand, no two of them agree. Barnes puts their bodies beneath the centre of the throne, sustaining it, with their heads facing outward so that from any quarter they appear to surround it. Ellicott places the crystal sea between the seer and the throne, and the creatures beyond it, encircling. Robertson takes the phrase as meaning what one sees from the front, one creature on each of the four sides. Wesley refers the first phrase to height and the second to the four quarters of the compass.

On the English word beasts they are of one mind and thoroughly out of patience. Barnes calls it a very unhappy translation of a word that means simply a living thing; Clarke traces the rendering to Wiclif, whom later translators followed, and remarks that a beast before the throne of God in heaven sounds oddly; Robertson notes that the Greek is not the word for wild animals at all. What the creatures are is another matter. Barnes argues that they can be neither angels nor men, since angels appear separately later and the elders are already human, and takes them as Ezekiel took his: symbols of the majesty and providential government of God, of vigilance, and of the energy with which His commands are executed. Robertson agrees they are kin to Ezekiel’s cherubim, though the faces and wings differ, and proposes that they stand for creation as the elders stand for the redeemed; their being full of eyes he takes for unlimited intelligence and the ceaseless vigilance of nature. Wesley calls them principal powers of heaven whose order cannot be determined, then advances a further scheme in which the elders represent the Jewish church and the living creatures the Christian, their number symbolising a gospel extended to all nations.
7:
Robertson fixes the limits of the comparison first: in Ezekiel every creature carries four faces, whereas here each bears one, and since the third is said to have a face as of a man the likeness in every instance reaches only to the face. Barnes had argued the same point from the same clue, and guessed that the bodies beneath were all of one form, most likely that of an ox, as best suited to bear a weight. Robertson takes the four together as representing whatever is noblest, strongest, wisest and swiftest in nature, and refuses to hunt a separate meaning in each face; he dismisses in particular the identification of the four with the four evangelists as an early and baseless invention. Clarke reports that same identification as Christian tradition — the eagle to John, the ox to Luke, the lion to Mark, the man to Matthew — and sets beside it a rabbinic account of the four standards of the camp of Israel, Judah’s lion to the east, Ephraim’s ox to the west, Reuben’s man to the south and Dan’s eagle to the north, which he says agrees with the faces of Ezekiel’s cherub. If the elders stood for the Jewish congregation, he concludes, these stand for the whole Christian Church. Wesley notes the same likeness to Ezekiel’s cherubim that supported the moving throne, and the difference from those over the mercy seat, which each had all four faces; and he passes on, without endorsing it, the opinion of a recent writer that those were emblems of the Trinity and of the incarnation of the second Person.

Ellicott presses the translation into an argument. To call these creatures beasts violates the laws of apocalyptic imagery, because in this book the wild beast is precisely the figure of brute force and unrestrained passion in the evil powers. These are rather representative of animated nature, four because four hold a primacy in the world — man among creatures, the eagle among birds, the ox among cattle, the lion among the untamed — and their qualities combine into one picture of true service, brave as the lion, patient as the ox, aspiring as the eagle, intelligent as man. He observes further that the number four in this book is almost always tied to the earth, as in its quarters, elements and seasons. On the eyes he gathers the prophetic parallels, the wheels of Ezekiel and the seven-eyed stone of Zechariah and the seven eyes of the Lamb, and rejects the suggestion that they signify unceasing praise; he prefers the reading that the power of nature is no blind force but bears everywhere the stamp of reason, and adds that its myriad eyes are fixed on God as the eyes of a servant on his master.

Barnes reads the faces as the attributes of a government rather than of nature. The lion is the monarch of the woods and so the emblem of dominion, signifying that the rule of Him upon the throne is absolute and entire; the young bullock, which is what the word properly means, signifies firmness and endurance and perseverance, and he supports this with a long survey of the bull and calf as objects of worship in Egypt and elsewhere, the calves Jeroboam set up at Dan and Bethel, and the winged bulls lately dug from the ruins of Nineveh. The human face he takes for intelligence, which is what distinguishes man from the creation beneath him, and thus for a divine administration founded on a clear knowledge of things rather than on blind fate or chance. Gill takes a wholly different road, making the lion the emblem of the ministers of the word: strong to endure hardness and to bear the infirmities of the weak, and bold to preach without fearing the faces of men.
8:
The six wings send every commentator to Isaiah’s seraphim, and there they divide over what the covered feet mean. Gill reads the two that cover the face as reverence in God’s presence, the two that cover the feet as a confessed sense of sinfulness and imperfection even in the best works and in the ministry of the word, and the two for flight as readiness to serve. Ellicott has the three pairs stand for reverence, humility and obedience. Wesley keeps the first pair for humility and reverence but takes the covered feet for readiness and diligence in executing divine commissions, which reverses the usual sense. Barnes refuses to speculate about how the wings were arranged, calling conjecture vain, then allows that two probably veiled the face and the rest served for flight. Robertson observes only that the number follows Isaiah rather than Ezekiel, where the creatures have four wings apiece.

Barnes corrects the English of the next clause: the word rendered about belongs with the eyes rather than the wings, so that the creatures are full of eyes around and within, which marks the universal vigilance of providence. Ellicott makes the same point practically — neither the raising nor the dropping of the wings obstructed their sight. Robertson locates the inner eyes under the wings and takes them for the secret energies of nature, and on the words they rest not he insists that God and Christ never cease their activity, so that the working of nature under God’s hand is itself a ceaseless tribute of praise. Wesley calls it a happy unrest, and adds that day and night is our way of speaking, since there is no night in heaven.

Over the threefold holy the readings run deep. Henry hears the creatures adore one God only, and three holies in that one God, the Holy Father, the Holy Son and the Holy Spirit, and says it was in this glory that the prophet saw Christ and spoke of him. Wesley works from the vocabulary: of the two words the English renders alike, one means properly merciful while this one signifies separated, and so denotes the excellence peculiar to God, who remains at an incomprehensible distance not only from all that is impure but from everything created. Holiness and Godhead therefore mean the same, and as a king is addressed by his majesty so Scripture speaks of God’s holiness; holiness is covered glory and glory uncovered holiness. He too finds the mystery of the Trinity confirmed here. Ellicott notes that one great manuscript repeats the word eight times, and that the clause about the whole earth being full of God’s glory, which Isaiah has, is missing; Wesley accounts for the omission by saying it is deferred until the enemies are destroyed and the glory does fill the earth. Ellicott also reports and declines a reading that would make the living beings the creative power of God rather than the creation itself, on the ground that the elders stand for the regenerate Church and not for the power that regenerates.

Clarke supplies the background rather than the exegesis, insisting that both the language and the imagery here are rabbinical. He translates a long passage in which four troops of angels stand about the throne, the divine presence in the midst with the incommunicable name upon the crown, and seraphim covering their faces lest they see that presence and their feet lest they discover its footstool. He adds a second rabbinic saying that four creatures hold principality in this world, man among the intelligent, the eagle among birds, the ox among cattle and the lion among wild beasts, all set beneath the throne so that no creature should exalt itself — the very scheme Ellicott had used on the previous verse without naming its source. These creatures, Clarke concludes, may be taken as representatives of the whole creation.
9:
Robertson reads the construction as a clause of repetition rather than of unbroken continuance: whenever the living creatures give glory, the elders answer. He treats the two acts as coordinated, and sums the arrangement in a phrase — created life adores the Uncreated — taking the creatures as the representatives of nature and the elders as the redeemed. He also records, without adopting it, that a modern editor takes the elders for angels rather than for redeemed men, which reopens a question left unsettled earlier in the chapter. Wesley reads the timing the same way, that as often as the creatures give glory the elders immediately fall, at the same instant and frequently; but he adds a distinction of posture and of address that no one else notices. The living creatures do not say Holy art thou to God directly; they only bend a little, out of deep reverence, and say that the Lord is holy. The elders, once they are fallen down, may say Worthy art thou, O Lord our God.

Barnes keeps to his reading of the whole vision as a picture of divine government. The creatures ascribe glory continually because the ways and acts of God in His providential rule are continually such as to honour Him; and the elders, being the representatives of the redeemed Church, join in, so that as often as there is a fresh manifestation of the principles of that government the church renders praise anew. Whatever is thought of the symbol, he says, the fact is not in doubt: the church of God always rejoices when His administration is newly displayed. The crowns are cast down in token that the wearers owe their triumph to Him and were crowned at all only by His merciful dealing. Clarke sets the gesture in its human context, as an allusion to the eastern custom of prostration and to the homage by which lesser kings acknowledged the supremacy of an emperor.

Gill keeps his own scheme steadily. The living creatures are the ministers of the gospel, who begin the worship of God and lead in it; the elders are the members of the churches, who follow and approach in the humblest manner. What the creatures ascribe, he says, is the glory of all God’s perfections, of His covenant and promises, of the gifts and grace bestowed on them and of the success of their ministry, and in doing so they glorify Father, Son and Spirit together, giving to each the due glory of election, redemption and sanctification. Henry turns the same scene directly on the reader. All true believers wholly ascribe their redemption and conversion, their present privileges and their future hopes to the eternal and most holy God; and if we on earth would do as they do, our praises must be constant and not interrupted, united and not divided, thankful and not cold and formal, humble and not self-confident.
11:
Two of them begin with the text itself. Gill reports that the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition, the Latin and all the Oriental versions read Thou art worthy, O Lord, and our God, to receive, and he explains the verb carefully: God cannot properly be said to receive glory and honour and power from His creatures except in the sense that they confess and declare these to belong to Him. Ellicott adopts the longer reading, sets the doxology out as a threefold ascription, and insists on a tense the English blurs — not that by God’s will all things are, but that they were, and were created. The existence of all things, he says, was owing to the will of God, and their creation was the realisation of that will. Robertson supports the same reading of the last clause from the grammar. The nominative stands here for a vocative, as when Thomas addressed the risen Christ; the articles before glory and honour point back to the previous verse, though power is added; the emphasis falls on the pronoun thou; and the aorist of the verb to create gives a summary picture of the whole act rather than of a process. The imperfect they were he takes as a cursory glance at the universe as a fact, and allows that it may point to a potential existence in God’s purpose in the eternal past, before the actual creation in time. Wesley reads the same words as meaning that they began to be, and takes the following clause to mean that they have continued in being ever since; it is to the free and gracious will of One who cannot possibly need anything that all things owe their first existence.

Barnes lays the doctrine out plainly. Man can confer no power on God, but he can acknowledge the power that is His and adore Him for its exercise. There is no other reason why the universe exists at all than that such was the will of God; He spoke and it was done, and whatever wisdom or power or goodness is manifest in the creation is the faint expression of what exists essentially in the Creator, so that it is right to look up through nature to nature’s God. The closing words he presses hard: the things that were created are not eternal and not self-existent, but were formed from nothing. Wesley finds in the threefold glory and honour and power a deliberate answer to the threefold holy of the living creatures, and adds that God receives this praise not only when He is thus praised but also when He destroys His enemies and glorifies Himself anew.

Clarke turns the doxology into an argument. All creation here acknowledges the supremacy of God, and the song teaches that He made all things for His pleasure and preserves them from the same motive. From this, he says, it is most evident that He hates nothing He has made, and could have made no intelligent creature with the design of rendering it eternally miserable; it is strange that the contrary supposition ever entered the heart of man, and high time that the benevolent nature of the Supreme God were vindicated from aspersions of that kind. The claim stands in the same chapter as Gill’s account of the elders ascribing to God the glory of election, and neither writer takes any notice of the other.
